summary: AI-Scientist is an unattended research pipeline: idea generation, a Semantic Scholar novelty check, an aider coding loop that runs experiments, a LaTeX writeup, and a 5-way ensemble paper review. Nobody waits on any single response - the experiments step alone has a 7200 s timeout - so the levers that matter are cost and resilience, not latency. Every LLM call funnels through ai_scientist/llm.py's create_client/get_response_from_llm, plus aider (LiteLLM), which the scanner cannot see. I vendored the runtime and wrapped all seven SDK client constructions (llm.py, both launchers, the ICLR reviewer benchmark), and added the LiteLLM install hook so aider's experiments and writeup traffic routes too. Three blockers then stood between 'wrapped' and 'routing': every gpt/o-series call sends seed=0, which Router's Responses API rejects (so none of the app's own 21 SDK requests in my probe reached Router - the single request that did was a direct LiteLLM call the probe made itself); the default --model claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and the hardcoded reviewer gpt-4o-2024-05-13 are retired ids absent from Router's catalog; and the Claude branch passed temperature= to client.messages.create(), which the installed anthropic 1.13.0 removed, so every Claude call - including the default - raised TypeError before any request left the process. I fixed the SDK break, dropped seed via router.policy.json, and mapped the three retired ids onto current catalog models that are cheaper than the ones they replace. Measured against the Router simulator, 12 of 15 probe requests now reach Router, and check --all reports 7 of 9 scanner-visible calls routing. What stays: the n>1 review ensemble (Responses has no n, and looping it costs ~2x on gpt-4o), the OpenRouter Llama path (Router has no Llama), the DeepSeek and Gemini clients (their own hosts, and their ids are not catalog ids), and aider on a Claude --model (LiteLLM only honours litellm.client_session on its OpenAI provider).
reviewed: I read every LLM call in the repo and costed the pipeline from the actual prompt sizes: the novelty check re-sends the whole of experiment.py (28.5 kB for nanoGPT) in its system prompt for up to 10 rounds x 50 ideas, and each review re-sends neurips_form plus a 61 kB few-shot paper ahead of the paper under review, 10 times per paper. That prefix waste is the biggest cost item in the app and it is mechanically fixable, so I built it: per-stage spend labels, per-stage prompt_cache_key, and explicit Anthropic cache_control breakpoints on both the system prompt and the growing conversation. Everything else turns on a quality judgement I cannot settle offline - which model each stage should run on, whether the 5-way ensemble and its 5 reflection rounds earn their cost, whether the citation loop's 20 rounds can become one structured pass - so those are proposals with the arithmetic and the exact policy to apply. I also dropped one improvement I had started: a fix to check_idea_novelty's enumerate(None) crash, because a side-by-side test showed the base code already sets papers_str before the crash and the broad handler resumes the same loop, so the error line is cosmetic and there are no tokens to save. No live Router evidence is in this report: no migration key was reachable in this session, so every router-live row is not-run.

calls.task: batch sampling for the review ensemble (n=n_responses)
every Claude call: idea generation, novelty check, citations, reviews
every gpt call: idea generation, novelty check, citations, reviews
the coding loop that writes and re-plans experiment.py (up to 4 iterations x 5 runs)
writes and refines each LaTeX section, ~50 whole-file passes per paper
LaTeX repair: missing citations, missing or duplicate figures, duplicate headers, chktex errors
rewrites the paper from the review (--improvement)

items.title: Route every OpenAI and Anthropic client the app builds
items.summary: Vendors router_runtime.py and passes all seven SDK client constructions through wrap_openai()/wrap_anthropic().
items.gains: One Router key for the app's OpenAI and Anthropic traffic, with per-request spend records, cross-vendor model choice and provider fallback. Inactive until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set; ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again.
items.price: no change on its own - the same models are requested; the price changes come from m5
items.why: Every LLM call in the repo reaches a client built in one of seven places: create_client() in ai_scientist/llm.py (the Anthropic client and the OpenAI client), the two hardcoded openai.OpenAI() reviewer clients in launch_scientist.py, the same two in experimental/launch_oe_scientist.py, and the client in review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py. Wrapping the constructions rather than the call sites leaves the code's own request shape untouched, so each request is still planned individually and anything Router cannot serve goes to the provider exactly as before. The runtime is vendored once at the repo root instead of once per package (the codemod's default), because every entry point already needs the repo root importable. In iclr_analysis.py I moved the generated import below its sys.path.append("../"), since that script runs from its own directory and the runtime would not have been importable above it.

evidence.detail: repo suite (compileall + import of 6 modules): 10 passed, matching the 10-passed baseline
check --run over a probe driving create_client/get_response_from_llm for 12 model choices: every wrapped client's requests reach the Router transport and are planned (trace lines for all of them)
no migration key was reachable in this session (`check --run --live` reported 'no migration key'), so nothing here is confirmed against api.router.com

items.title: Route aider's LiteLLM calls (experiments and writeup)
items.summary: ai_scientist/llm.py calls router_runtime.install_litellm() at import, which every entry point reaches before aider builds a Coder.
items.gains: The app's largest token consumer routes. aider drives the experiments loop (up to 4 iterations x 5 runs, each carrying experiment.py and notes.txt) and roughly 50 whole-file LaTeX passes per paper - far more tokens than the calls the scanner can see.
items.price: no change - same models, same requests
items.why: aider reaches providers through LiteLLM, so no client construction exists for the scanner to find. install_litellm() sets litellm.client_session, which LiteLLM's OpenAI provider reads when it builds its SDK client (litellm/llms/openai/common_utils.py:223), putting the Router transport underneath. The hook lives in ai_scientist/llm.py because every entry point imports it - launch_scientist.py, launch_oe_scientist.py and perform_writeup.py's main - and it short-circuits on active() before importing litellm, so it costs nothing when Router is off. Scope limit: LiteLLM's Anthropic provider does not read client_session, so aider on a Claude --model still goes straight to Anthropic (item s4).

evidence.detail: a probe importing aider first and ai_scientist.llm second (launch_scientist.py's order), then driving a real Coder.run() over a temp file: gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini each reach Router on /v1/responses, with the trace naming ai_scientist/llm.py:<module> as the client origin
the same probe with --model claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and claude-sonnet-5: 0 requests reach Router and no trace line is produced at all - LiteLLM's Anthropic path never consults the transport
10 passed; the hook adds no import cost while RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is unset
no migration key in this session

items.title: Fix the Claude path for the installed Anthropic SDK
items.summary: client.messages.create() no longer accepts temperature=, so the kwarg is sent only on SDKs whose signature still has it.
items.gains: The Claude path runs at all. Before this, every Claude call - including the default --model claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and every claude row of AVAILABLE_LLMS - raised TypeError inside the SDK before a request was built, so there was nothing to route.
items.loses: temperature=0.75 on Claude calls under anthropic >= 1.x, which has no sampling-temperature parameter at all (its replacement is output_config.effort). Idea generation and the review ensemble rely on temperature for diversity, so Claude-served samples will be less varied than the code intends. Older anthropic releases keep their exact behaviour: the kwarg is still sent where the signature accepts it.
items.why: Measured on the installed anthropic 1.13.0: inspect.signature(Messages.create) has no `temperature` (it has max_tokens, system, thinking, output_config, service_tier and others). Reproduced end to end - a probe calling get_response_from_llm with any claude model raised 'TypeError: Messages.create() got an unexpected keyword argument temperature'. requirements.txt pins no anthropic version, so a capability check is the right fix: it repairs the installed SDK without regressing older ones. This is a pre-existing break at the base commit, not something the migration introduced, but the Claude path cannot be migrated without it.

evidence.detail: inspect.signature(anthropic.resources.messages.Messages.create) on anthropic 1.13.0 has no temperature parameter; the app's own code path raised TypeError before the fix
after the fix the same probe issues real HTTP requests for claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and -20241022 (previously zero requests), and all 8 stage-probe requests are accepted on /v1/messages
10 passed

items.title: Drop `seed` so the OpenAI calls can route
items.summary: router.policy.json drops seed from the Router-bound copy of each request; the original request is untouched.
items.gains: Unblocks every gpt and o-series call in the app. With the clients wrapped but seed still present, every one of the app's 21 OpenAI-SDK probe requests traced as 'untranslatable: seed' and went to OpenAI unchanged; the only request that reached Router in that run was a direct LiteLLM call the probe made itself. This is the single change that turns the OpenAI half of the migration on.
items.loses: The best-effort seed=0 reproducibility hint on routed requests. OpenAI documented seed as best-effort only and never guaranteed determinism, and these calls run at temperature 0.75 (0.1 for reviews), so no reproducibility that exists today is given up - but a team that was relying on seed for run-to-run comparison no longer has even the hint on routed traffic.
items.why: ai_scientist/llm.py sends seed=0 on three of its OpenAI branches. Router's Responses API returns 400 for seed, so the runtime keeps those requests on the provider rather than silently changing them. Dropping it in policy rather than in code means the provider-bound copy still carries seed: if Router refuses a request and the runtime retries at OpenAI, OpenAI gets exactly what the code built. Undo by removing "drop_params" from router.policy.json and running `router-migrate policy` - router_policy.py is generated, so reverting the commit alone is not enough if other policy changes have landed since.

evidence.detail: before: all gpt/o-series probe requests traced as 'provider / untranslatable: seed'. after: the same calls trace as 'chat' and arrive at the simulator on /v1/responses
10 passed
no price effect; seed is free

items.title: Serve the app's three retired model ids from the catalog
items.summary: Maps claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620/-20241022 to claude-sonnet-5 and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 to gpt-4o on Router-bound requests.
items.gains: Routes the two paths that actually carry production traffic: the default --model for launch_scientist.py, and the reviewer model hardcoded in both launchers. Both replacements are cheaper than what they stand in for - claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10 against Claude 3.5 Sonnet's $3/$15, gpt-4o $2.50/$10 against gpt-4o-2024-05-13's $5/$15 per 1M tokens - so the review and ideation stages get cheaper as well as current.
items.loses: The exact 2024 model weights. These are different models: idea quality, novelty verdicts and review scores will all shift, and the ICLR reviewer accuracy numbers in review_iclr_bench were measured against gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and no longer describe what the reviewer does. Router's catalog does not carry the originals (confirmed against the live catalog snapshot), so the alternative is leaving the app's default path off Router entirely.
items.price: cheaper: -33% input / -33% output on the Claude path, -50% input on the reviewer path, at list prices from the live catalog
items.why: Router serves only catalog ids and maps 22 dated snapshots back to catalog ids - gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 among them, but not gpt-4o-2024-05-13, and no claude-3-5-sonnet at all. claude-sonnet-5 is the nearest current Sonnet; I chose it over claude-sonnet-5-5 (same $2/$10) because it is the id Router's own measurements and price table use. Temperature support did not constrain the choice once m3 landed, since the installed SDK no longer sends temperature on this surface - without m3 a temperature-less target would have been required (claude-sonnet-5 is temperature:false in the catalog). The map applies only to Router-bound requests: with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY unset the code still asks its provider for the id it always asked for. Undo by removing "model_map" from router.policy.json and running `router-migrate policy`.

evidence.detail: check --run: requests for claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and -20241022 arrive as model=claude-sonnet-5 on /v1/messages; gpt-4o-2024-05-13 arrives as model=gpt-4o on /v1/responses. 12 of 15 probe requests reach Router, 12 valid 0 invalid

live catalog snapshot (GET /v1/models, 2026-10-14): claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10/$0.20-cached, gpt-4o $2.50/$10/$1.25-cached. The retired ids are absent from that snapshot, which is why they could not route

no quality comparison was run: Claude 3.5 Sonnet and gpt-4o-2024-05-13 are not reachable through Router, so there is nothing to compare against. review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py is the repo's own instrument for this and needs ~500 real reviews
10 passed

items.title: The OpenRouter Llama path stays on OpenRouter
items.summary: Router's catalog has no Llama model, so llama3.1-405b cannot be served without substituting a different model family.
items.why: create_client builds an OpenAI-SDK client pointed at openrouter.ai for --model llama3.1-405b. Two things keep it off Router: the host is not api.openai.com (the runtime only plans OpenAI and Anthropic hosts unless a client is wrapped with unlock_hosts, which the fact sheet marks as customer-approved), and meta-llama/llama-3.1-405b-instruct is not a catalog id - the live catalog has no Llama entry at all. `check` suggests mapping it to gpt-3.5-turbo; that would substitute a deprecated 2023 model for a 405B instruct model, which is not a swap anyone asked for. Left alone. OPENROUTER_API_KEY must stay configured for this --model to work.

evidence.detail: check --run with --model llama3.1-405b: 3 requests to openrouter.ai:443, none to Router, no transport trace (the client is not wrapped)
no Llama model in the live catalog snapshot (100 ids)

items.title: The DeepSeek and Gemini clients stay with their vendors
items.summary: Both point at their own hosts and their ids are not catalog ids; Router's Gemini entries additionally need the caller's own Google key.
items.why: deepseek-chat, deepseek-coder, deepseek-reasoner and every gemini-1.5/2.0/2.5 id in AVAILABLE_LLMS are absent from Router's catalog. Router does carry DeepSeek under provider-agnostic ids (deepseek-v4-flash $0.13/$0.26, deepseek-v4.1-flash $0.30/$1.20) and Gemini under vertex ids, but reaching them would need a host unlock plus a model substitution for DeepSeek, and a caller-owned Google credential for Gemini (requires_byok: true on all 13 vertex entries) - neither is a migration-safe change. DEEPSEEK_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY must stay configured for these --model choices. See i2 for the consolidation proposal.

evidence.detail: check --run with --model deepseek-chat / deepseek-reasoner / gemini-2.0-flash: 6 requests to api.deepseek.com and 3 to generativelanguage.googleapis.com, none to Router, no transport trace. `check --all` reports these three sites as routing, which is a scanner artefact - it credits them to the wrapped OpenAI client, but create_client builds separate unwrapped clients for these base URLs
live catalog: no deepseek-chat/-coder/-reasoner and no gemini-1.5/2.0 ids; all 13 vertex gemini entries are requires_byok

items.title: The n>1 review ensemble stays on OpenAI
items.summary: Responses has no `n`, and looping the 5 samples instead would roughly double the review stage's input cost on gpt-4o.
items.why: perform_review calls get_batch_responses_from_llm with n_responses=5 (both launchers pass num_reviews_ensemble=5), and the gpt branch sends that as n=5. Router's Responses API has no n, so the runtime reports 'untranslatable: n' and OpenAI serves it. The obvious port - loop five single calls, which is already what the non-gpt branch does - is not free: n=5 bills the ~19k-token prefix once, five separate calls bill it five times, and gpt-4o's cache only discounts repeats by 50% ($1.25 against $2.50 per 1M). Estimated from the actual prompt sizes that is about $0.24 against $0.11 per paper. Coverage is not worth doubling the cost of the most expensive stage in an unattended pipeline. This is worth revisiting on a deep-cache model, where the same loop becomes cheaper than n=5 - see i3. One consequence worth stating plainly: the ensemble call is the FIRST call perform_review makes, so although the meta-review and all 5 reflection rounds do route, none of them is reached unless OpenAI serves the ensemble call first. The review stage therefore still depends on OPENAI_API_KEY being configured and on OpenAI being reachable - which is part of why i5 proposes fallbacks on this stage.

evidence.detail: check --run: get_batch_responses_from_llm(n_responses=5) traces as 'provider / untranslatable: n' (with seed dropped, n is the only remaining blocker); n_responses=1 routes

perform_review driven end to end with launch_scientist.py's exact reviewer arguments: at num_reviews_ensemble=5 the first call stays on the provider and the stage gets no further; at num_reviews_ensemble=1 the review and its first reflection both arrive at Router (2 valid, 0 invalid) and the run then stops only because the simulator's canned reply is not a review JSON
estimated from prompt bytes - neurips_form plus the 61 kB few-shot paper is ~19k tokens of identical prefix; 4 extra cached reads at gpt-4o's $1.25/1M against one uncached pass at $2.50/1M

items.title: aider on a Claude --model stays on Anthropic
items.summary: LiteLLM reads litellm.client_session only on its OpenAI provider, so the Router transport is never consulted for Anthropic traffic.
items.why: This is the one material gap in the migration, and it is in the heaviest stage. With the default --model claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, aider runs the experiments loop and the whole LaTeX writeup against Anthropic directly - more tokens than everything the scanner sees. install_litellm() cannot help: litellm.client_session is read in litellm/llms/openai/common_utils.py, and the Anthropic handler builds its own HTTP client. Confirmed by probe: aider with claude-sonnet-5 (a valid catalog id) still produces zero Router requests and no transport trace. Pointing aider at Router natively does not work either - LiteLLM's OpenAI provider calls /v1/chat/completions, which Router answers with a plain-text 404. The route that does work is choosing an OpenAI-family model for the aider steps, which is i4.

evidence.detail: real Coder.run() probe: gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini reach Router; claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 and claude-sonnet-5 produce 0 Router requests and no trace line
litellm 1.81.10: grep finds litellm.client_session read in llms/openai/common_utils.py:223 and llms/azure/*, and nowhere under llms/anthropic/

items.title: Label each stage; stop re-paying for identical prefixes
items.summary: Per-stage spend labels, per-stage prompt_cache_key, and Anthropic cache_control on both the system prompt and the growing conversation.
items.gains: Cuts the dominant cost in this pipeline and makes spend legible per stage. The prefixes are enormous and re-sent constantly: the novelty check's system prompt is the task description plus the whole of experiment.py (28.5 kB ~ 7.1k tokens for nanoGPT) for up to 10 rounds x 50 ideas; each review re-sends neurips_form plus a 61 kB few-shot paper (~15.3k tokens) ahead of the paper, across 5 ensemble members, the meta-review and 5 reflection rounds; and every reflection loop re-sends the entire conversation each round, which for the novelty stage reaches ~20k tokens by round 10 - roughly 5M input tokens per 50-idea run. Cached reads cost a tenth of input on claude-sonnet-5 ($0.20 against $2.00 per 1M): that one stage goes from about $10 a run to about $1. Router's measured gpt-4o-mini case is -49% on a 9,020-token prompt. The labels are the second half of the value: spend now breaks down by ideate / novelty / review / review_reflect / review_meta / cite instead of arriving as one bucket, and every later tuning decision (model per stage, tier per stage, fallbacks per stage) becomes a router.policy.json edit with no code change. I verified that per-stage model_map works and resolves correctly.
items.loses: Nothing functional. Each labelled request carries one extra header, which providers ignore. The Claude system prompt becomes a one-element block list, which the Messages API accepts either way. A cache write bills above a plain input token, so a stage whose prefix is below Anthropic's ~1k-token minimum and never repeats pays a few percent more - of the six stages only `ideate` has a short system prompt, and its user prompt carries experiment.py so the conversation breakpoint still pays. allow_flex_tier is set on all six stages but is inert for the models the app selects today: gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1 have no Flex tier and the runtime's guard logs 'allow_flex_tier skipped'. It starts paying (-50% measured on gpt-5.4-mini) only once a gpt-5.x/gpt-6.x/o3/o4-mini model is selected, which is i2.
items.why: Router makes caching and attribution cheap, but neither works on this app as written: without an app-supplied label every call in the repo is one feature (ai_scientist/llm.py:get_response_from_llm), so one prompt_cache_key would be shared by six unrelated prefixes and policy could not distinguish the stages; and policy fields do not apply on /v1/messages at all (only model_map and drop_params do), so Claude-surface caching has to be explicit in the request. The branch does all three: feature= threaded through both llm.py entry points and sent as x-router-migrate-feature, named at all 11 call sites; prompt_cache_key: "$feature" plus metadata.team in policy; and two cache_control breakpoints on the Anthropic path. The conversation breakpoint copies down to the marked block so the caller's history never accumulates breakpoints - a fifth one is a 400 from Anthropic, and this loop would have added one per round.

evidence.detail: check --run: 8 of 8 probe requests valid on both surfaces, each arriving under its own label (feature=ideate, novelty, review, review_reflect, review_meta, cite), unlabelled calls still working and falling back to file:function

policy_for() per stage and _apply_policy() on a request body: prompt_cache_key resolves to the stage name, metadata.team is added, and allow_flex_tier is applied on gpt-5.4-mini and correctly skipped on gpt-4o

5 simulated reflection rounds over a fake Anthropic client: exactly 2 cache breakpoints per request as the history grows from 1 to 9 messages, no cache_control in the history handed back to the caller, cached_messages() does not mutate its input
10 passed on the branch
no migration key in this session, so the cache-hit rates and the Flex discount are Router's published measurements rather than this app's

items.title: Modernise the model choices and tier them per stage
items.summary: Replace the 2024-era model list with current catalog models and give each pipeline stage the model its task actually needs.
items.gains: The largest cost lever left, and it also activates the Flex tier. Estimated from the real prompt sizes for a 50-idea run: the novelty check is ~500 calls at ~15k input tokens, about 7.5M tokens - $15 at claude-sonnet-5's $2/1M, about $0.75 at claude-haiku-5-5's $0.10/1M. It is a search-and-judge task over paper abstracts, not a creative one, and it is by far the highest-volume stage. Citation selection (pick indices out of 10 abstracts, ~40 calls) is the same shape: gpt-5.4-mini at $0.75/$4.50 with Flex is roughly a tenth of today's cost. Ideation is where capability is worth paying for and should stay Sonnet-class. Separately, AVAILABLE_LLMS is a menu of 44 ids of which 7 route and most no longer exist at either provider (o1-preview, o1-mini, gemini-1.5/2.0, the bedrock and vertex rows); it should become a short list of ids Router actually serves, which also removes the dated-id problem m5 patches over.
items.loses: Model identity, stage by stage - every one of these is a quality bet with no offline measurement behind it. A cheaper novelty judge that wrongly calls an idea novel sends the pipeline into hours of GPU experiments; one that wrongly calls it stale discards good work. Trimming AVAILABLE_LLMS removes --model choices someone may be using, including the Bedrock and Vertex paths that bypass Router entirely.
items.why: With i1's labels in place this is a router.policy.json edit, no code change: give each stage a features.<stage> entry with its own model_map and allow_flex_tier. One implementation detail I verified and that will bite otherwise: policy merges layer by layer per key, so a features.<stage>.model_map REPLACES defaults.model_map rather than merging - I confirmed that gpt-4o-2024-05-13 resolves to None under a stage that defines its own map. Each per-stage map must therefore repeat whichever m5 entries it still needs. Suggested starting point: novelty -> claude-haiku-5-5 ($0.10/$0.50) or gpt-5.4-mini; cite -> gpt-5.4-mini ($0.75/$4.50, Flex-eligible); ideate -> keep claude-sonnet-5; review -> gpt-5.4 ($2.50/$15) or keep gpt-4o until the benchmark says otherwise. Two things to do before committing to the numbers: turn on shadow models, which records cost and latency for up to 3 candidates on a 5-10% sample of real /v1/responses traffic (needs content recording, not available on BYOK keys), and run review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py for the review stage, which is the repo's own accuracy/F1/AUC instrument against real ICLR decisions. Both are human actions on app.router.com and a benchmark run, which is why this is proposed rather than built.

items.title: Give aider its own model so the heaviest stage routes
items.summary: Add a --coder-model for the aider steps, defaulting to an OpenAI-family coding model, instead of reusing --model.
items.gains: Puts the app's biggest token consumer on Router. Today aider inherits --model, so the default Claude choice keeps the experiments loop and all ~50 whole-file LaTeX passes per paper on Anthropic, outside Router's routing, spend records and fallbacks (item s4). An OpenAI-family coder goes through litellm.client_session and routes today, with no further work. It is also better design on its own terms: writing and debugging experiment.py is a different task from inventing research ideas or judging novelty, and there is no reason one flag should pick the model for both.
items.loses: The default coder model changes, so the code aider writes and the LaTeX it edits will differ - this is the stage whose output decides whether an experiment runs at all, so it is the highest-variance change in this report. Anyone who deliberately chose Claude for coding has to pass --coder-model to keep it. It also adds a flag to a CLI that currently has one model knob.
items.why: Three routes exist and only one is safe. (a) This one: aider on an OpenAI-provider model id, which routes through the runtime's Chat-to-Responses translation and still works if Router is off, because OpenAI serves the id directly. (b) Point aider at Router natively - does not work: LiteLLM's OpenAI provider calls /v1/chat/completions, which Router answers with a plain-text 404. (c) Use a model id like openai/claude-sonnet-5 so LiteLLM's OpenAI provider carries a Claude catalog id to Router, which the fact sheet confirms works (the OpenAI SDK served Claude). That one is tempting but makes the app Router-dependent: with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY unset the request goes to OpenAI and 404s, and the runtime's provider fallback only triggers when Router itself refuses. To build: add --coder-model to both launchers and perform_writeup's main, thread it to the two Model(...) constructions in each, default it to a current OpenAI coding model (gpt-5.3-codex $1.75/$14 - note the fact sheet records a 403 data_residency_mismatch for that id on one test account, so check it against this key first, with gpt-5.4 as the fallback choice), and label the aider traffic so i1's policy can tier it.

items.title: Rebuild the review: the ensemble and its reflections are mostly waste
items.summary: 11 full-paper calls per review produce 9 averaged integers and one synthesised text; cut the ensemble onto a deep-cache model and shorten the reflections.
items.gains: The review stage is roughly 500 calls a run at ~19k input tokens each and it is structurally redundant. perform_review samples 5 reviews at temperature 0.75, asks a meta-reviewer to synthesise them, then overwrites every numeric field with the arithmetic mean of the ensemble - so the meta-review's scores are computed and thrown away, and only its prose survives. Then 4 reflection rounds re-derive the whole review, scores included, from the averaged one. Two independent wins: run the ensemble as 5 independent calls on a model with a real cache discount (gpt-5.4-mini: $0.75 input, $0.075 cached - 1 uncached pass plus 4 cached reads is ~$0.020 against ~$0.048 for n=5 on gpt-4o) which is both cheaper AND routable, closing item s3; and cut the reflection rounds, which are the least defensible calls in the app.
items.loses: Review scores and decisions change, and the reviewer is the product here - review_iclr_bench exists precisely to measure it. Fewer reflection rounds may lose genuine self-correction; a cheaper ensemble model may shift the accept/reject balance. This must not ship on reasoning alone.
items.why: Deliberately framed as rework and not built, because the acceptance test is already in the repo: review_iclr_bench/iclr_analysis.py scores reviewer accuracy, F1 and AUC against real ICLR decisions over ~500 papers. The right sequence is to measure the current configuration, then each variant - ensemble 5 vs 3, reflections 5 vs 2 vs 0, gpt-4o vs gpt-5.4-mini vs claude-sonnet-5 - and keep whatever holds accuracy at the lowest cost. That run needs a Router key and real spend, so it is a decision for a human with a budget, not an offline change. Note the review path also has a latent crash to fix while in there: when every ensemble member omits a scored field, scores is empty and int(round(np.mean([]))) raises on a nan.

items.title: Collapse the 20-round citation loop into one structured pass
items.summary: perform_writeup makes 20 rounds x 2 LLM calls plus 20 aider passes, each carrying the entire LaTeX draft, to add at most 20 citations.
items.gains: The second-largest block of writeup tokens after the section passes. Each of the 40 LLM calls embeds the whole draft (which grows all run, past 10k tokens), and each round yields at most one citation. Asking for N citation needs in a single structured-output call, searching all the queries, then making one aider pass per accepted citation would cut the LLM calls from ~40 to ~2 and the draft re-sends with them. Router serves structured outputs across vendors (responses.parse with Pydantic works on both gpt-4o and Claude), so the mechanism is available on whatever model the stage ends up on.
items.loses: The loop's iterative character: today each round sees the draft as amended by the previous round, so it can notice a paragraph that is now over-cited or a citation that landed badly. A single pass plans all its citations against the original draft. Citation quality and placement would change, and references.bib correctness is load-bearing for whether the paper compiles.
items.why: This is the clearest instance in the app of an LLM loop doing work that one structured call plus deterministic code could do: the search is already deterministic (search_for_papers), the selection is already an index list parsed out of JSON ("Selected": "[0, 1]"), and the bibtex insertion is already a string replace. Only the 'where should this cite go' step needs a model. Rework rather than change because num_cite_rounds=20 is a quality dial someone chose, and the paper's citation count and placement is visible output.

items.title: Drop the second whole-paper refinement loop
items.summary: perform_writeup refines every section once as it is written, then refines all 8 sections again at the end.
items.gains: About 8 of roughly 50 whole-file aider passes per paper, each carrying template.tex plus experiment.py plus notes.txt - call it a sixth of the writeup stage's tokens, on the stage that (with i4) is the app's largest. The first refinement_prompt already asks for exactly the same error classes as second_refinement_prompt; the second loop's only genuinely new instruction is cross-section consistency and cutting redundancy, which applies to maybe two or three sections rather than all eight.
items.loses: Cross-section polish. The second loop is the only pass that sees the finished paper as a whole, so dropping it entirely will leave some repeated figures and duplicated prose that it would have caught. A middle option is keeping it for Abstract, Introduction and Related Work - the sections whose job is to describe the rest - and dropping it for the other five.
items.why: Cheap to try and easy to judge, because the output is a PDF a human can read. Worth instrumenting before deciding: the refinement prompts tell the model to answer 'I am done' when there is nothing to change, so logging how often each pass actually edits the file would settle it with data instead of taste. Same instrument applies to NUM_REFLECTIONS=3 in idea generation and num_reflections=5 in review.

items.title: Fall over to another vendor on the stages that cost hours to redo
items.summary: A cross-vendor `models` list on review and writeup, so one 500 from a provider does not discard a finished experiment.
items.gains: Protects the expensive end of the pipeline. A failed review call raises, perform_review propagates, do_idea returns False, and the idea is discarded - after its experiments have already burned GPU hours. The backoff decorator only retries RateLimitError and APITimeoutError, so a 500 or a 503 ends the idea. A ranked candidate list on Responses lets Router fall through to another vendor silently; the fact sheet confirms cross-vendor fallback works (gpt-5-nano to claude-haiku-4-5).
items.loses: Flex on the same stage: the runtime drops allow_flex_tier when fallbacks apply, so a stage cannot have both - that is why this is scoped to review and writeup rather than set as a default. The response does not say which candidate served, so cost per call becomes less predictable, and the least capable candidate in the list caps structured output, tools and context for every request on that stage. Truncated attempts are billed even when a later candidate answers.
items.why: Needs i1's labels first: without them every call in the app shares one feature, so fallbacks would apply to all of them and would silently disable Flex everywhere. With labels it is two features.<stage>.fallbacks entries. Worth noting what is NOT measured: Router's fallback behaviour on real provider outages (5xx, 429) is documented but unmeasured, so this buys documented insurance, not proven insurance.

items.title: Raise the output cap for reasoning models
items.summary: MAX_NUM_TOKENS=4096 is shared by every model, but on o1/o3 the reasoning tokens come out of that same budget.
items.gains: Stops reasoning-model runs from silently dropping work. The o1/o3 branch sends max_completion_tokens=4096, and reasoning tokens count against it, so a model that thinks for 3k tokens has 1k left for a review JSON. Router reports those responses as incomplete with no text (and 0 tokens, $0), extract_json_between_markers returns None, the assert fires, and the idea or review is discarded by the surrounding except. The same cap is also near Claude's floor: reasoning.effort on Claude needs roughly 1,100 output tokens or more or Router returns 400.
items.loses: A higher cap means more output tokens billed when a model does use the room, and output is the expensive half (o3 $8/1M, gpt-5.4 $15/1M). It also lets a runaway generation run longer before it is cut off.
items.why: Not built because I could not measure the right number: no migration key was reachable, so I could not see how many reasoning tokens these prompts actually consume on o3 or gpt-5.x, and picking a figure by feel is how a quiet cost increase gets shipped. The fix is to make the cap per-model-class rather than one constant - roughly 16k for reasoning models, 4096 elsewhere - and to log usage.reasoning_tokens from a few real calls first. Related, and nearly free: the branch order in get_response_from_llm tests 'gpt' in model before the o1/o3 branch, so a future gpt-5 choice would take the gpt path and be sent temperature, which Router rejects for every model the catalog marks temperature:false (36 of them). The runtime drops it for routed requests; a provider-bound request would 400.

items.title: Put a spend cap on the key and turn on shadow models
items.summary: Two settings on app.router.com: a per-key cap, and shadow sampling to measure candidate models on real traffic.
items.gains: A cost ceiling this app does not have anywhere in code. launch_scientist.py defaults to --num-ideas 50 and runs unattended for hours, up to 8 parallel workers, with no budget check in any loop - and with --improvement it runs the writeup and the 5-way review twice per idea. A per-key spend cap is the only backstop; requests return 401 once it is reached. Shadow models then answers the questions i2 and i3 cannot answer offline, by recording cost and latency for up to 3 candidate models on a 5-10% sample of real /v1/responses traffic.
items.loses: A cap that trips mid-run turns into 401s, which this app surfaces as discarded ideas rather than as a clear 'out of budget' - so the cap needs to be set with a full run's cost in mind, and the failure mode is worth a log line in do_idea. Shadow models requires content recording to be enabled on the account, is not available on BYOK keys, and records cost and latency only - not quality.
items.why: Both are human actions on the Router dashboard, not code, which is why this is proposed with no branch. Worth doing before i2 rather than after: shadow sampling is how the model-tiering decision gets evidence, and the cap is how a wrong tiering decision stays cheap. Note that spend caps apply after usage is recorded, so concurrent requests can overshoot - with --parallel up to 8, expect the cap to be a soft ceiling.

items.title: Try Switchyard on the aider coding loop
items.summary: model: "switchyard" picks a cheap model for easy turns and a capable one for hard turns within a conversation.
items.gains: The experiments loop is exactly what Switchyard is documented for - the docs call it experimental and aimed at coding agents. Its turns vary enormously in difficulty: 'the run failed with this traceback' and 'implement the next item on your list' do not need the same model, and today both get whichever model --model named. The writeup loop has the same shape, where 'fix this chktex warning' sits next to 'write the Results section'.
items.loses: Quality on non-coding work is unmeasured, and the writeup is not coding. Per-call model choice moves out of the repo and into a saved strategy on app.router.com, so the app's behaviour changes when someone edits that strategy - with nothing in the diff to show it. Listed at $3/$15, above several models the stages would otherwise use, so it is not automatically cheaper.
items.why: Depends on i4: the strategy is reached through the OpenAI surface, so the aider steps have to be on an OpenAI-provider model id first. A human must save a Switchyard strategy (efficient_model / capable_model) on app.router.com before model: "switchyard" does anything - the fact sheet confirms it then works from app code and served gpt-5.6-luna at Flex. Worth trying on the experiments loop alone, measured by how often experiments complete inside MAX_ITERS, before considering it for the writeup.

items.title: Make the deterministic LaTeX repairs deterministic
items.summary: generate_latex detects duplicate figures and duplicate section headers with regexes, then asks an LLM to fix what it already found.
items.gains: Removes up to three whole-file LLM round-trips per paper, each carrying template.tex plus experiment.py plus notes.txt. The detection is already exact - re.findall over \includegraphics and \section, then a count - so nothing about finding the problem needs a model. Dropping a repeated \includegraphics block and a repeated \section line is ordinary text editing.
items.loses: Judgement about which copy to keep. The prompts ask the model to 'identify the best location for the figure and remove any other', and placement genuinely matters in a two-column paper - code would keep the first occurrence, which is not always right. Editing .tex with regexes also risks breaking a figure environment in a way the LLM would not, and a broken .tex means no PDF at all.
items.why: Ranked last of the improvements because the money is small (these calls only fire when duplicates exist) and the downside is a paper that does not compile. The safe form is narrow: de-duplicate exact repeated \section{...} lines in code, leave figures to the model, and keep the chktex loop as it is - that one is a genuine repair task. Worth doing only once something is measuring how often each repair path fires.

items.title: search_for_papers retries HTTP errors forever
items.summary: backoff.on_exception with no max_tries or max_time means a persistent 429 or 403 from Semantic Scholar hangs the novelty stage indefinitely.
items.why: Not a Router or LLM issue, but it gates the stage this report spends most of its attention on, so it should not go unsaid. ai_scientist/generate_ideas.py decorates search_for_papers with @backoff.on_exception(backoff.expo, requests.exceptions.HTTPError) and sets no bound, so with no S2_API_KEY configured - which is the default, since S2_API_KEY is read with os.getenv and never required - a steady stream of 429s becomes an unbounded exponential-backoff loop inside check_idea_novelty with no timeout above it. The fix is a max_time or max_tries and treating exhaustion as 'no papers found'. Found while costing the novelty stage; not changed, because it is outside the migration and wants its own test.

evidence.detail: ai_scientist/generate_ideas.py: the decorator passes only backoff.expo, the exception type and on_backoff - no max_tries, no max_time, and no timeout= on the requests.get it wraps

items.title: No live Router evidence in this report
items.summary: No migration key was reachable, so every router-live evidence row is not-run and the simulator is the only end-to-end check.
items.why: `router-migrate check --run CMD --live` answered 'error: no migration key' throughout this session, even though the ledger records live: true. Everything claimed here is therefore one of three things, and each evidence row says which: measured against the local Router simulator through this app's own code (routing decisions, request shapes, model rewriting, labels, cache breakpoints); taken from the live catalog snapshot in .router-migrate/catalog_live.json (prices, which ids exist, temperature and BYOK flags, dated-id coverage); or quoted from Router's own published measurements (the -49% gpt-4o-mini cache case, 10,350 cached tokens on Claude, -50% Flex on gpt-5.4-mini). What that leaves unconfirmed for this app specifically: that claude-sonnet-5 accepts these exact requests on /v1/messages, the real cache-hit rate on these prefixes, this app's Flex discount, and whether Router's spend views pick up the x-router-migrate-feature header on Messages traffic - which is the surface the Claude path uses, and which carries no metadata.feature. Three short live calls would settle the first; i8's shadow sampling settles the rest.

evidence.detail: check --run --live: 'error: no migration key'

items.title: Undoing a policy trade-off needs a recompile
items.summary: router_policy.py is generated from router.policy.json; reverting m4 or m5 by git alone can leave a stale compiled copy.
items.why: m4 (drop seed) and m5 (the model map) are both entries in defaults in a single JSON object, and the runtime reads the compiled router_policy.py beside it, not the JSON. Reverting one commit touches the same two files the other commit touched, and the compiled file is one JSON line, so a selective revert will conflict there. The reliable undo is to edit router.policy.json by hand and run `router-migrate policy`, which rewrites and re-hashes the compiled copy - the outside check fails on a stale one. Setting ROUTER_MIGRATE_POLICY=off disables the whole policy without touching files, which turns off m4 and m5 together and so returns the OpenAI calls and the default Claude path to their providers.

evidence.detail: router_policy.py holds the whole policy as a single json.loads('...') line plus a POLICY_HASH; `router-migrate policy` regenerated it cleanly after each hand edit in this session
